newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea seeks leap forward through labour reform.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea seeks leap forward through labour reform.

text.p: South Korea on Tuesday proposed new labour laws to remove a legacy of authoritarian control and help companies improve competitiveness.

Prime Minister Lee Soo-sung said in a statement broadcast on television that providing labour laws designed to establish new labour-management relations was the "task directly affecting the nation's destiny".

"We stand at a crossroads leading to becoming a wealthier, prosperous nation or a nation without any hope falling behind others," he said after presiding over a cabinet meeting that confirmed a government draft for labour reform.
Lee urged workers and businessmen to bury mistrust and start anew but both labour and management groups immediately expressed dissatisfaction, with unionists threatening strikes.

The proposal lifts the ban on trade unions' political activity and allows outside intervention in labour disputes, while removing restrictions barring workers from forming more than one union in each workplace from the year 2002.

Teachers will be permitted to organise a solidarity group for limited collective bargaining from 1999, but they would still be barred from going on strike. Public servants would not be allowed to form unions.
Economists said ending fierce confrontations between unions and management was crucial for improving South Korea's competitiveness.

Since South Korea started introducing democratic reforms a decade ago, violent industrial conflict has become almost an annual affair, with companies often halting production for weeks because of strikes.

The proposal follows South Korea's recent invitation to join the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD). South Korea's parliament last week ratified the nation's membership in the Paris-based club of established economies.
The revision, worked out after seven months, would allow firms to lay off employees in order to introduce new technology, improve productivity and end management difficulties.
Companies, however, must attempt to avoid layoffs and inform workers at least 60 days beforehand if a reduction in the number of employees becomes inevitable.

The revision clarifies that workers can no longer claim wages during the period they are on strike. Many South Korean companies have paid wages to striking workers to improve union-management relations.
Companies no longer have to pay unionists who concentrate their work on labour issues and not for their companies.
The Korean Confederation of Trade Unions, currently outlawed but active with about 500,000 members, said in a statement the reform tended to reflect management interests.
"We will hold a meeting tomorrow to discuss starting general strikes," it added.
The Korea Employers' Federation said in a statement: "The decision to permit more than one union at a workplace must be reconsidered in view of our country's labour conditions."
It said rival unions would seek to take radical steps to attract more membership.
The government said it planned to send a labour reform bill to parliament later this month for approval.
